newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: N.Korea says 134 children dead in food crisis - UN.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea says 134 children dead in food crisis - UN.

text.p: North Korea told international aid agencies on Tuesday that 134 children have died from malnutrition in the country's mounting food crisis, a United Nations official said.

Hans Olsen of the Children's Fund UNICEF told a news briefing the figure was provided by a North Korean Health Ministry official to local representatives of U.N. and other aid organisations at a meeting in Pyongyang.
(Earlier, UNICEF said the meeting had taken place on Monday, but later corrected this.)

It was believed to be the first time the secretive communist state, badly hit by two harvest failures due to heavy rains and flooding in 1995 and 1996, had given any statistics on mortality from the resulting food shortages.
UNICEF later quoted the Health Ministry official as saying 15.3 per cent of all children in North Korea were now directly affected by malnutrition.
Olsen said UNICEF officials in the country had just returned from Huichon City north-east of Pyongyang where they found all food supplies had stopped to nurseries and kindergartens.

"The situation is clearly getting worse very quickly," said Olsen, speaking a few hours after the U.N.'s Department of Humanitarian Affairs (DHA) in New York had made a global appeal for $126.2 million to help stave off famine in North Korea.

"The situation can be described as a humanitarian disaster in the making," DHA chief Yasushi Akashi told a New York news conference to launch the appeal, drafted in consultation with the Pyongyang government.

At Tuesday's Geneva briefing, the U.N.'s World Food Programme (WFP), the main agency involved in getting supplies into North Korea, said the agency was coming to the conclusion that "famine is virtually inevitable in the coming months".
WFP spokeswoman Christiane Berthiaume said food arriving in response to earlier U.N. appeals was far from enough to meet the needs of the country, which has a population of some 24 million.

Last week, WFP Executive Director Catherine Bertini told a news conference in Seoul after touring the North that it needed $95 million -- more than double the sum it had sought in earlier appeals -- to help feed hungry babies and small children.

Bertini said she had seen many children in nurseries showing signs of advanced malnutrition. Unless emergency aid arrived soon, she added, by the summer there would be large-scale malnutrition and deaths.

The WFP appeal forms part of the DHA total. The remaining $31 million would go to help North Korea resume normal food production and restore basic health services disrupted by the floods, which destroyed roads and housing as well as crops.
